questions.q: Which region of the medulla oblongata serves as the primary excitatory vasomotor pressor area sending tonic sympathetic drive to preganglionic neurons in the spinal intermediolateral cell column?
options: Caudal ventrolateral medulla
Nucleus ambiguus
Rostral ventrolateral medulla
Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
questions.explain: Glutamatergic and C1 adrenergic neurons in the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) project directly to sympathetic preganglionic neurons (T1-L2) to maintain tonic vasoconstrictor and cardioacceleratory tone.

open.q: Name the excitatory medullary pressor area that sends tonic sympathetic drive to spinal preganglionic neurons.
accept: Rostral ventrolateral medulla
RVLM

questions.q: Which medullary nucleus receives primary visceral sensory afferents from arterial baroreceptors, cardiopulmonary mechanoreceptors, and peripheral chemoreceptors via cranial nerves IX and X?
options: Nucleus ambiguus
Nucleus tractus solitarius
Caudal ventrolateral medulla
Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
questions.explain: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the dorsomedial medulla is the primary integration hub for baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents, coordinating both vagal excitation and sympathetic inhibition.

open.q: Which brainstem nucleus is the first central synapse for baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents carried by cranial nerves IX and X?
accept: Nucleus tractus solitarius
NTS
Solitary tract nucleus

questions.q: How does activation of the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) by high arterial blood pressure suppress sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow from the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM)?
options: The NTS excites GABAergic neurons in the CVLM, which then inhibit the RVLM
The NTS inhibits the preganglionic neurons of the intermediolateral column directly
The NTS excites neurons in the nucleus ambiguus that go on to inhibit the RVLM
The NTS excites the RVLM, which then drives vagal outflow to the heart
questions.explain: Baroreceptor-activated NTS neurons excite inhibitory GABAergic neurons in the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM). These neurons inhibit rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) pressor neurons, reducing sympathetic vasomotor tone.

open.q: Describe the synaptic pathway connecting the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) to the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) during baroreceptor activation.
accept: NTS excites inhibitory GABAergic neurons in the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM), which inhibit the RVLM
NTS activates CVLM GABAergic interneurons to suppress RVLM

questions.q: Which two medullary nuclei contain the preganglionic parasympathetic cardioinhibitory vagal neurons that slow heart rate?
options: Nucleus tractus solitarius and nucleus ambiguus
Rostral ventrolateral medulla and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
Hypoglossal nucleus and caudal ventrolateral medulla
Nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
questions.explain: The nucleus ambiguus (providing the bulk of rapid beat-to-beat myelinated B-fiber vagal chronotropic control to the SA node) and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus mediate parasympathetic cardioinhibition.

open.q: Name the two medullary nuclei that give rise to parasympathetic cardioinhibitory vagal fibers.
accept: Nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
Nucleus ambiguus and dorsal vagal nucleus

questions.q: How does bilateral vagotomy (cutting both vagus nerves) alter resting heart rate in a healthy adult, and what does this demonstrate?
options: It falls below 40 bpm, showing that sympathetic tone normally keeps the SA node firing
It stays unchanged, showing that vagal tone is minimal in a healthy resting adult
It rises toward the intrinsic SA-node rate, showing that vagal tone normally slows the heart at rest
It rises to about 150 bpm, showing that the SA node normally fires at that rate
questions.explain: At rest, tonic vagal acetylcholine release slows the SA node below its intrinsic rate of approximately 100–110 beats/min. Bilateral vagotomy removes this restraint and allows the rate to rise toward the intrinsic pacemaker rate.

open.q: What happens to resting heart rate when both vagus nerves are blocked with atropine or severed, and what physiological principle does this illustrate?
accept: Heart rate increases to ~100-110 bpm, demonstrating tonic parasympathetic (vagal) dominance at rest
HR rises to the intrinsic SA nodal rate (~100 bpm), showing resting vagal tone

questions.q: Which vascular receptor subtype mediates sympathetic vasoconstriction in skin, splanchnic, and renal arterioles, and which receptor mediates epinephrine-induced vasodilation in skeletal muscle arterioles?
options: Beta-1 causes vasoconstriction; M3 causes skeletal-muscle vasodilation
Alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction; beta-2 causes skeletal-muscle vasodilation
Alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction; beta-1 causes skeletal-muscle vasodilation
Beta-2 causes vasoconstriction; alpha-1 causes skeletal-muscle vasodilation
questions.explain: Norepinephrine activates vascular alpha-1 receptors, increasing smooth-muscle intracellular Ca2+ and causing vasoconstriction. Circulating epinephrine can activate beta-2 receptors in skeletal-muscle arterioles, increasing cAMP and promoting vasodilation.

open.q: Identify the adrenergic receptor subtype responsible for sympathetic vasoconstriction and the subtype responsible for epinephrine-mediated vasodilation in skeletal muscle arterioles.
accept: Alpha-1 for vasoconstriction and beta-2 for vasodilation
Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors constrict; beta-2 adrenergic receptors dilate

questions.q: What is Dale's vasomotor reversal phenomenon when intravenous epinephrine is administered before versus after an alpha-adrenergic antagonist (such as phentolamine)?
options: Alpha-blockade unmasks beta-2 vasodilation, so epinephrine lowers blood pressure
Alpha-blockade unmasks beta-1 stimulation, so epinephrine raises blood pressure further
Alpha-blockade turns epinephrine's depressor response into a pressor response
Alpha-blockade blocks beta-2 receptors too, so epinephrine has no effect on blood pressure
questions.explain: Epinephrine normally stimulates alpha-1 vasoconstriction as well as beta-2 vasodilation. After alpha-receptor blockade, beta-2-mediated vasodilation predominates and the pressor response is reversed to a depressor response (Dale's vasomotor reversal).

open.q: Explain Dale's vasomotor reversal observed when epinephrine is injected after alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade.
accept: Alpha-blockade prevents alpha-1 vasoconstriction and unmasks beta-2 vasodilation, converting epinephrine's pressor response into a fall in blood pressure
Unopposed beta-2 vasodilation lowers blood pressure instead of raising it

questions.q: Over which mean arterial pressure (MAP) range are the carotid sinus baroreceptors most sensitive and effective at buffering acute pressure fluctuations?
options: 20 to 50 mmHg
30 to 60 mmHg
180 to 250 mmHg
60 to 180 mmHg
questions.explain: Carotid sinus baroreceptors begin firing around 50-60 mmHg, reach maximal sensitivity around 90-100 mmHg (responding to both mean pressure and rate of pressure change dP/dt), and saturate above ~180 mmHg.

open.q: State the operating pressure range of the carotid sinus baroreceptors and the mean arterial pressure at which their sensitivity is greatest.
accept: 60 to 180 mmHg, with peak sensitivity around 90 to 100 mmHg
50-180 mmHg; most sensitive near normal resting MAP (~95-100 mmHg)

questions.q: Why are arterial baroreceptors ineffective at preventing chronic sustained hypertension over weeks or years?
options: Baroreceptor afferent fibres in the glossopharyngeal nerve degenerate under sustained high pressure
Neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius gradually lose their input from the vagus nerve
Baroreceptors reset within 1 to 2 days and fire at a normal rate despite the higher pressure
Baroreceptors become hypersensitive and drive sympathetic outflow even higher
questions.explain: Within 24 to 48 hours of sustained pressure elevation, baroreceptor firing rate returns toward baseline (baroreceptor resetting), making them short-term buffers of acute pressure swings rather than long-term pressure regulators.

open.q: Why do arterial baroreceptors fail to correct chronic long-term hypertension?
accept: They adapt or reset to the higher pressure level within 1 to 2 days
Baroreceptor resetting occurs during sustained pressure elevation

questions.q: What cardiovascular response is produced by firm external massage of the carotid sinus in the neck?
options: Reduced baroreceptor firing causes tachycardia and a rise in blood pressure within seconds
Increased baroreceptor firing causes bradycardia and a fall in blood pressure
Carotid body stimulation causes hyperventilation and vasoconstriction
Vagal withdrawal causes tachycardia and a rise in cardiac output
questions.explain: Carotid sinus massage stretches the baroreceptor endings, increasing afferent firing through cranial nerve IX to the NTS. This increases vagal activity and reduces sympathetic outflow, producing reflex bradycardia and sometimes hypotension.

open.q: What happens to heart rate and blood pressure during carotid sinus massage, and why?
accept: Heart rate and blood pressure decrease because mechanical stretch activates baroreceptors, increasing vagal tone and inhibiting sympathetic outflow
Reflex bradycardia and hypotension due to baroreceptor stretch activation

questions.q: Where are low-pressure cardiopulmonary volume receptors located, and what hormonal/renal responses occur when central blood volume expansion stretches them?
options: Atria and pulmonary veins; ADH and renal sympathetic activity fall, ANP rises
Aortic arch and carotid sinus; renin and aldosterone release rise
Atria and pulmonary veins; ADH and renin rise, ANP falls
Renal afferent arterioles; renin release falls and ANP rises
questions.explain: Cardiopulmonary low-pressure stretch receptors detect central blood-volume expansion. Their activation suppresses ADH and renal sympathetic activity and promotes atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) release, favouring water and sodium excretion.

open.q: Describe the renal and hormonal responses triggered when increased central blood volume stretches low-pressure atrial and cardiopulmonary volume receptors.
accept: Decreased ADH secretion, decreased renal sympathetic activity/renin, and increased ANP release causing diuresis and natriuresis
Suppression of ADH and RAAS plus ANP secretion to excrete excess water and sodium

questions.q: What is the Bezold-Jarisch reflex, triggered by stimulation of ventricular chemosensitive and mechanosensitive C-fiber receptors (such as during acute inferior myocardial infarction)?
options: Tachycardia, hypertension and hyperpnoea
Bradycardia, hypertension and bronchodilation
Tachycardia, hypotension and bronchoconstriction
Bradycardia, hypotension and apnoea
questions.explain: Stimulation of ventricular vagal C-fibre endings can produce the Bezold–Jarisch reflex: increased vagal activity and sympathetic withdrawal cause bradycardia and hypotension, often accompanied by respiratory inhibition.

open.q: State the classic triad of cardiovascular and respiratory responses in the Bezold-Jarisch reflex.
accept: Bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea (or hypopnea)
Reflex bradycardia, peripheral vasodilation (hypotension), and shallow breathing/apnea

questions.q: When arterial pressure is severely reduced, how can peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies help support blood pressure?
options: Low flow silences chemoreceptor afferents, so sympathetic vasoconstrictor output falls
Low flow raises chemoreceptor firing, which activates vagal outflow and lowers heart rate and cardiac output
Low flow causes local hypoxia and acidosis, increasing afferent drive to sympathetic centres
Low flow raises PCO2 and pH, which inhibits the medullary vasomotor centre
questions.explain: Severe hypotension reduces perfusion of the carotid and aortic bodies. Local hypoxia and accumulation of CO2 and H+ stimulate chemoreceptor afferents through cranial nerves IX and X, reinforcing medullary sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity.

open.q: How do peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond when severe hypotension reduces their blood flow?
accept: Local hypoxia and hypercapnia stimulate chemoreceptors to activate the medullary pressor center and increase sympathetic vasoconstriction
They excite the RVLM to raise sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone

questions.q: What is the direct cardiac response to carotid-body chemoreceptor stimulation during apnoea, and how may lung inflation modify the response when breathing continues?
options: Tachycardia through sympathetic activation, which lung inflation increases further
Bradycardia through vagal activation, which lung inflation can override to produce tachycardia
Bradycardia through vagal activation, which lung inflation increases further
Tachycardia through vagal withdrawal, which lung inflation converts into bradycardia
questions.explain: Carotid-body chemoreceptor activation can directly increase vagal cardioinhibitory activity and slow the heart, especially during apnoea. When breathing continues, pulmonary stretch-receptor input associated with lung inflation can inhibit vagal tone and produce a secondary tachycardic response.

open.q: Contrast the direct heart rate response to carotid body chemoreceptor stimulation during apnea versus when hyperventilation occurs.
accept: Direct stimulation causes bradycardia (during apnea), whereas pulmonary stretch receptors during hyperventilation cause secondary tachycardia
Primary bradycardia vs secondary tachycardia from lung inflation

questions.q: What are the four physiological phases of arterial blood pressure and heart rate during a standardized Valsalva maneuver (forced expiration against a closed glottis)?
options: I: pressure rises; II: pressure falls with tachycardia; III: brief dip; IV: overshoot with bradycardia
I: pressure falls; II: pressure rises with bradycardia; III: brief rise; IV: overshoot with tachycardia
I: pressure rises; II: pressure falls with bradycardia; III: brief dip; IV: overshoot with tachycardia
I: pressure rises; II: pressure stays high with tachycardia; III: brief dip; IV: undershoot with bradycardia
questions.explain: High intrathoracic pressure (~40 mmHg) initially squeezes the thoracic aorta (Phase I BP rise), then impedes venous return so BP falls and baroreceptors trigger tachycardia and vasoconstriction (Phase II); releasing strain drops intrathoracic pressure (Phase III dip), and restored venous return into constricted vessels produces a Phase IV BP overshoot and reflex bradycardia.

open.q: Explain why arterial blood pressure overshoots baseline and heart rate slows during Phase IV immediately after releasing a Valsalva maneuver.
accept: Restored venous return is pumped into an arterial tree still constricted by Phase II sympathetic tone, raising BP and triggering baroreceptor bradycardia
Surge in cardiac output meets persistent peripheral vasoconstriction, causing a hypertensive overshoot and reflex vagal bradycardia

questions.q: How is orthostatic hypotension defined, and what autonomic abnormality commonly causes the neurogenic form?
options: A fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing, from excessive vagal tone
A rise of 20 mmHg systolic within 3 minutes of standing, from excessive sympathetic discharge
A fall of 5 mmHg systolic within 3 minutes of standing, from loss of parasympathetic tone
A fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing, from impaired sympathetic vasoconstriction
questions.explain: Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. Normally, baroreceptor unloading increases sympathetic activity, causing tachycardia and alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension results when this compensatory autonomic response is impaired.

open.q: State the blood pressure criteria defining orthostatic hypotension within 3 minutes of standing.
accept: Drop in systolic BP >= 20 mmHg or diastolic BP >= 10 mmHg
Systolic decrease of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic decrease of at least 10 mmHg

questions.q: Through which two distinct receptor subtypes does arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone, ADH) regulate arterial blood pressure and body fluid volume?
options: V1 receptors increase renal water reabsorption; V2 receptors cause vasoconstriction
V1 receptors cause vasoconstriction; V2 receptors stimulate aldosterone release
V1 receptors cause vasoconstriction; V2 receptors increase renal water reabsorption
V2 receptors cause vasoconstriction; V3 receptors increase renal water reabsorption
questions.explain: ADH acts on V1 receptors (Gq/IP3) in vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction and on V2 receptors (Gs/cAMP) in renal collecting-duct principal cells to insert aquaporin-2 channels and increase water reabsorption.

open.q: Contrast the receptor subtypes, second messengers, and physiological actions of vasopressin (ADH) on blood vessels versus renal collecting ducts.
accept: V1 receptors (Gq/IP3) cause vascular smooth muscle vasoconstriction; V2 receptors (Gs/cAMP) insert aquaporin-2 channels in collecting ducts for water reabsorption
V1 mediates vasoconstriction via IP3/Ca2+; V2 mediates renal water retention via cAMP

questions.q: Which stimulus triggers the release of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) from cardiac myocytes, and how is plasma BNP used clinically?
options: Reduced renal perfusion; a raised level supports a diagnosis of renal artery stenosis
Ventricular wall stretch; a raised level supports a diagnosis of heart failure
Ventricular wall stretch; a raised level supports a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction
Hypoxia of atrial myocytes; a raised level supports a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism
questions.explain: Ventricular myocytes release BNP in response to increased wall stretch from pressure or volume overload. BNP and NT-proBNP levels support the diagnosis and assessment of heart failure, including in patients presenting with dyspnoea.

open.q: What mechanical stimulus releases B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) from the heart, and what is its major clinical diagnostic utility?
accept: Ventricular myocardial stretch/volume overload; diagnosing and assessing severity of heart failure
Ventricular wall stretch; biomarker for congestive heart failure

questions.q: Why do patients taking angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (such as lisinopril or enalapril) sometimes develop a persistent dry cough or angioedema?
options: Bradykinin accumulates because ACE normally breaks it down
Angiotensin I accumulates and directly stimulates bronchial sensory nerves
Histamine release from mast cells rises because ACE normally suppresses it
Direct beta-2 receptor blockade in the airway causes bronchospasm
questions.explain: ACE also acts as kininase II, degrading bradykinin. ACE inhibition therefore increases bradykinin, which can sensitise airway sensory nerves (dry cough) and increase vascular permeability (angioedema).

open.q: Explain the biochemical mechanism responsible for the dry cough side effect of ACE inhibitors.
accept: ACE inhibition blocks degradation of bradykinin (since ACE is kininase II), causing bradykinin accumulation in the airways
Accumulation of bradykinin due to inhibition of kininase II (ACE)

questions.q: What is 'central command' at the onset of voluntary exercise?
options: Muscle afferents signal metabolite build-up to the medulla once exercise is under way and work has begun
Carotid body firing rises as arterial PO2 falls early in exercise
Atrial stretch receptors detect rising venous return and speed up the heart
Motor cortex signals activate cardiovascular centres before muscle metabolites build up
questions.explain: At the onset or even anticipation of voluntary exercise, collateral signals from motor areas activate cardiovascular centres. This reduces vagal restraint and increases sympathetic drive, raising heart rate and contractility before metabolites from active muscles accumulate.

open.q: Define 'central command' in the cardiovascular regulation of exercise.
accept: Feedforward signals from higher motor centers to medullary cardiovascular centers at the onset of exercise that reduce vagal tone and increase sympathetic activity
Cortical motor drive to the brainstem increasing heart rate and sympathetic outflow immediately upon starting exercise

questions.q: During dynamic aerobic exercise, how do systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and pulse pressure change?
options: Systolic pressure rises, diastolic rises equally, and pulse pressure is unchanged
Systolic pressure falls, diastolic rises, and pulse pressure narrows
Systolic pressure rises, diastolic changes little, and pulse pressure widens
Systolic and diastolic pressures both rise sharply, and pulse pressure narrows
questions.explain: Increased CO drives systolic BP up (often to 160-180 mmHg), whereas massive metabolic vasodilation in active skeletal muscles lowers TPR enough to keep diastolic BP flat or slightly reduced (~70-80 mmHg), producing a wide pulse pressure.

open.q: Describe how systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and pulse pressure change during dynamic isotonic exercise.
accept: Systolic BP increases markedly, diastolic BP stays unchanged or decreases slightly, and pulse pressure widens
High systolic BP, stable/slightly lower diastolic BP, widened pulse pressure

questions.q: How is cardiac output redistributed among major organ beds during strenuous dynamic exercise compared to rest?
options: Muscle, renal and splanchnic flow rise; skin flow falls; cerebral flow is maintained
Muscle, coronary and skin flow rise; renal and splanchnic flow fall; cerebral flow is maintained
Muscle and cerebral flow rise several-fold; coronary and skin flow fall; renal flow is maintained
Muscle flow rises; coronary, cerebral and skin flow fall; renal and splanchnic flow rise
questions.explain: During strenuous dynamic exercise, blood flow increases to active skeletal muscle, the myocardium and (for heat loss) the skin. Sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces renal and splanchnic flow, while cerebral blood flow is relatively maintained.

open.q: How does blood flow distribution to skeletal muscle, heart, brain, and splanchnic/renal organs change during strenuous aerobic exercise?
accept: Skeletal muscle and coronary blood flow increase markedly, splanchnic and renal blood flow decrease, and cerebral blood flow remains constant
Increased muscle and coronary perfusion, decreased gut and kidney perfusion, unchanged brain perfusion

questions.sub: Cardiovascular Response to Hemorrhage and Shock
questions.q: In a patient who acutely loses 1,000 mL (~20%) of blood volume, which sequence of compensatory neurohumoral mechanisms helps restore arterial blood pressure?
options: Baroreceptor unloading raises sympathetic activity, followed by RAAS and ADH activation and fluid shift into capillaries
Baroreceptor loading raises vagal activity, followed by ANP release and fluid shift out of capillaries
Baroreceptor unloading raises vagal activity, followed by ANP release and renal sodium loss
Chemoreceptor suppression lowers sympathetic activity, followed by RAAS inhibition and ADH withdrawal
questions.explain: Hemorrhage unloads arterial and cardiopulmonary baroreceptors, triggering rapid sympathetic vasoconstriction/tachycardia, RAAS/ADH retention of salt and water, and Starling-force absorption of interstitial fluid into capillaries (lowering hematocrit over hours).

open.q: Explain why a patient's hematocrit is initially normal immediately after an acute hemorrhage but falls over the next 12 to 24 hours even without intravenous fluid administration.
accept: Arteriolar constriction lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, drawing protein-free interstitial fluid into capillaries (transcapillary refill) and diluting red blood cells
Capillary fluid shift from the interstitial space into plasma hemodilutes the remaining red cells

questions.sub: Cardiovascular Response to Hemorrhage and Shock
questions.q: Why does preferential sympathetic alpha-1 vasoconstriction during hemorrhagic shock spare the cerebral and coronary circulations?
options: Vagal vasodilation offsets alpha-1 constriction in the cerebral and coronary vessels
Circulating vasopressin selectively dilates cerebral and coronary arterioles during shock
These vessels lack sympathetic nerves and are controlled by the vagus nerve instead
Local metabolic autoregulation overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction in these vessels
questions.explain: Cerebral and coronary perfusion are protected mainly by powerful local autoregulatory mechanisms, including responses to CO2, H+, adenosine and other metabolites. Sympathetic vasoconstriction is less dominant in these beds than in skin, gut and kidneys.

open.q: Why are cerebral and coronary blood flows preserved during the intense sympathetic vasoconstrictor response to hemorrhagic shock?
accept: Cerebral and coronary vessels have few alpha-1 receptors and are controlled primarily by local metabolic autoregulation
Sparse alpha-adrenergic vasoconstrictor innervation and strong local metabolic autoregulation

questions.sub: Cardiovascular Response to Hemorrhage and Shock
questions.q: Which mechanisms drive decompensated (irreversible) hemorrhagic shock when severe hypotension persists uncorrected?
options: Adrenal catecholamine stores are exhausted, so vasoconstriction fails while cardiac output stays normal
Baroreceptors reset to the lower pressure, so sympathetic drive is switched off and vasodilation follows
Acidosis and hypoxia blunt vascular responses to catecholamines, and myocardial depression lowers output further
Aldosterone and ADH levels fall sharply, so renal water loss reduces blood volume further
questions.explain: In progressive/irreversible shock, positive feedback vicious cycles take over: coronary hypoperfusion weakens the heart, ischemic capillary damage leaks plasma, acidosis paralyzes precapillary sphincters while postcapillary venules remain constricted (pooling blood), and gut translocation triggers sepsis.

open.q: Identify two positive-feedback vicious cycles that cause compensated hemorrhagic shock to progress into irreversible shock.
accept: Coronary hypoperfusion causing myocardial depression, and tissue acidosis/hypoxia causing precapillary vasodilation and capillary fluid leakage
Myocardial ischemia reducing cardiac output and ischemic endothelial injury/endotoxemia causing vasomotor collapse

questions.q: What is the mammalian diving reflex triggered by breath-holding (apnea) combined with cold water contact on the face (ophthalmic/maxillary trigeminal nerve afferents)?
options: Tachycardia, peripheral vasodilation and falling blood pressure
Bradycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and rising blood pressure
Bradycardia, peripheral vasodilation and falling blood pressure
Tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and rising blood pressure
questions.explain: Cold facial stimulation carried by trigeminal afferents, together with apnoea, activates vagal output to the heart (bradycardia) and sympathetic vasoconstriction in peripheral beds. This helps conserve oxygen for the heart and brain.

open.q: State the stimulus and three physiological responses of the mammalian diving reflex.
accept: Cold water on the face with breath-holding; causes apnea, vagal bradycardia, and peripheral sympathetic vasoconstriction
Trigeminal cold stimulation + apnea -> bradycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, and apnea

questions.q: What autonomic shift produces neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope in response to severe emotional distress, pain, or prolonged motionless standing?
options: Sympathetic withdrawal with vasodilation, together with increased vagal activity and bradycardia
Sympathetic surge with vasoconstriction, together with vagal withdrawal and tachycardia
Sympathetic withdrawal with vasodilation, together with vagal withdrawal and tachycardia
Sympathetic surge with vasoconstriction, together with increased vagal activity and marked bradycardia
questions.explain: Vigorous contraction of an underfilled left ventricle (during prolonged standing or emotional catecholamine surge) triggers ventricular mechanoreceptors (Bezold-Jarisch-like pathway), abruptly inhibiting RVLM sympathetic tone and exciting vagal cardioinhibition so MAP drops below cerebral autoregulation (~60 mmHg).

open.q: Describe the autonomic mechanism that causes transient loss of consciousness in vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) syncope.
accept: Sudden sympathetic withdrawal (vasodilation) combined with vagal surge (bradycardia), dropping blood pressure and cerebral blood flow
Paradoxical vasodepressor hypotension and cardioinhibitory bradycardia reducing cerebral perfusion

questions.q: Which vascular beds lack functional parasympathetic vasodilator innervation and rely almost exclusively on variations in sympathetic tone and local metabolic factors?
options: Salivary glands and erectile tissue of the genitalia
Gastric mucosa and exocrine pancreas
Nasal mucosa, lacrimal glands and parotid gland
Skeletal muscle, kidneys and most systemic resistance arterioles
questions.explain: Parasympathetic cholinergic vasodilator fibers innervate only specialized beds (salivary/GI glands, erectile tissues via pelvic splanchnic NO/ACh, and certain cranial vessels); systemic blood pressure and TPR are controlled by sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone.

open.q: Name two specialized vascular beds in the body that receive direct parasympathetic vasodilator innervation.
accept: Salivary glands and erectile tissue (corpora cavernosa)
Genital erectile tissue and gastrointestinal/salivary glands

questions.q: A 39-year-old woman presents with episodic headaches, profuse sweating, palpitations, and paroxysmal hypertension (BP 220/126 mmHg). Plasma free metanephrines are markedly elevated, and abdominal CT identifies a 4 cm right adrenal medullary pheochromocytoma. Why must an alpha-adrenergic blocker (such as phenoxybenzamine) be started BEFORE administering a beta-blocker?
options: Beta-blockade first raises catecholamine release from the tumour
Alpha-blockade must come first because phenoxybenzamine inhibits catecholamine synthesis in the tumour
Beta-blockade first removes beta-2 vasodilation and leaves alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed
Beta-blockade first causes severe bradycardia that alpha-blockade cannot reverse
questions.explain: In catecholamine excess, beta-2-mediated vasodilation partly offsets alpha-1 vasoconstriction. Alpha blockade must therefore be established before beta blockade; otherwise, blocking beta-2 first can leave severe alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed and precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

open.q: Why is initiating beta-blocker monotherapy before alpha-adrenergic blockade contraindicated in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
accept: Blocking beta-2 vasodilation leaves alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed, causing severe hypertensive crisis
Unopposed alpha-1 receptor stimulation triggers life-threatening hypertension

questions.q: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after a bee sting with stridor, diffuse urticaria, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 68/38 mmHg (anaphylactic shock). Intramuscular epinephrine rapidly reverses his hypotension and airway edema by acting on which adrenergic receptors?
options: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction and beta-1 cardiac stimulation, with no effect on the airway
Alpha-1 vasoconstriction, beta-1 cardiac stimulation and beta-2 bronchodilation
Beta-1 cardiac stimulation and beta-2 bronchodilation, with no effect on blood vessels
Alpha-2 vasoconstriction, M3 bronchodilation and D1 renal vasodilation
questions.explain: Epinephrine is the first-line lifesaving drug in anaphylaxis because its non-selective agonist activity simultaneously restores TPR (alpha-1), augments CO (beta-1), relieves bronchospasm (beta-2), and suppresses further mast-cell histamine release (beta-2 cAMP).

open.q: Explain how epinephrine's actions on alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors reverse the life-threatening features of anaphylactic shock.
accept: Alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction to restore BP, beta-1 increases cardiac output, and beta-2 causes bronchodilation and inhibits mast cell degranulation
Alpha-1 raises TPR/reduces edema, beta-1 boosts HR/contractility, beta-2 dilates bronchi and stabilizes mast cells

questions.q: A person stands suddenly from a lying position. The initial fall in arterial pressure reduces stretch of which receptors, leading to increased sympathetic outflow?
options: Carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors
Carotid body and aortic body chemoreceptors
Muscle mechanoreceptors in the lower limbs
Pulmonary stretch receptors in the lung parenchyma
questions.explain: Reduced arterial pressure decreases stretch and firing of carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors. The medullary cardiovascular centres respond by increasing sympathetic and reducing parasympathetic activity, raising heart rate, contractility and peripheral resistance.

open.q: Which arterial baroreceptors detect the initial fall in blood pressure on standing?
accept: carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors
carotid and aortic baroreceptors

questions.q: A patient with severe bilateral carotid sinus hypersensitivity develops marked bradycardia and hypotension when a tight collar is applied. Which reflex pathway best explains this response?
options: Reduced carotid sinus firing raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal outflow
Raised carotid body firing lowers sympathetic outflow and raises vagal outflow
Raised pulmonary stretch receptor firing raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal outflow
Raised carotid sinus firing lowers sympathetic outflow and raises vagal outflow
questions.explain: Excessive stretch of the carotid sinus increases glossopharyngeal afferent firing to the nucleus tractus solitarius, increasing vagal activity and inhibiting sympathetic outflow.

questions.q: A patient with a high cervical spinal cord injury has profound hypotension and bradycardia due to loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone. Which mechanism contributes most directly to this pattern?
options: Loss of parasympathetic supply to the sinoatrial node and vascular smooth muscle
Excess vagal tone from loss of inhibitory input to the nucleus ambiguus
Interruption of descending sympathetic pathways to spinal preganglionic neurons
Direct damage to the carotid sinus baroreceptors and their glossopharyngeal afferents
questions.explain: A high spinal cord lesion can interrupt descending control of sympathetic preganglionic neurons, causing vasodilation and venous pooling; unopposed vagal influence may produce bradycardia.

questions.sub: Clinical application: Cardiovascular response to exercise
questions.q: At the onset of dynamic exercise, heart rate rises before substantial changes in blood gases occur. Which mechanism contributes to this rapid initial increase?
options: Fall in venous return activating atrial stretch receptors
Central command causing vagal withdrawal and sympathetic activation
Rise in arterial baroreceptor firing producing sympathetic activation
Early rise in arterial PCO2 stimulating the carotid bodies
questions.explain: Central command from higher motor centres and early vagal withdrawal rapidly increase heart rate at exercise onset, followed by increased sympathetic drive as exercise continues.

questions.sub: Clinical application: Cardiovascular response to exercise
questions.q: During sustained dynamic exercise, a trained athlete maintains arterial pressure despite a large rise in cardiac output and skeletal-muscle blood flow. Which adjustment helps prevent excessive hypotension?
options: Increased sympathetic vasoconstriction in the less active vascular beds
Dilation of renal and splanchnic arterioles to offload the heart
Withdrawal of sympathetic tone from the skin and splanchnic circulation
A fall in stroke volume, which offsets the rise in heart rate
questions.explain: Sympathetic vasoconstriction in renal and splanchnic beds, together with local metabolic vasodilation in active muscle, redistributes flow while helping maintain systemic arterial pressure.

questions.q: A patient with septic shock has warm extremities, low systemic vascular resistance and hypotension early in the illness. Which vascular mechanism is most responsible?
options: Widespread alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction from excess catecholamines
Hypovolaemia from haemorrhage with compensatory venoconstriction
Acute loss of myocardial contractility causing cardiogenic pooling
Widespread vasodilation driven by inflammatory mediators such as nitric oxide
questions.explain: Inflammatory mediators, including nitric oxide, cause widespread vasodilation and reduced systemic vascular resistance in distributive septic shock; capillary leak and myocardial dysfunction may also contribute.
